message.content:
For outdoor garden sculptures the choice of stone balances **durability**, **carving ability** and **cost**:

| Stone | Weather‑resistance | Carving difficulty | Typical cost | Best use case |
|-------|--------------------|--------------------|--------------|---------------|
| **Granite** | Very high – resists freeze–thaw, erosion, UV | Hardest to carve (requires diamond tools) | Medium‑high | Large, coarse‑detail pieces that need minimal upkeep |
| **Limestone** | Good – can soften in acid rain, but still weather‑resistant | Easy to carve (soft when freshly quarried) | Low‑medium | Fine detail, classic look; may need sealing in acidic climates |
| **Marble** | Moderate – susceptible to staining, acid damage | Very easy to carve | High | Highly detailed, elegant pieces; requires regular cleaning/sealing |
| **Sandstone** | Variable – softer, more porous | Easy to carve | Low | Textured, rustic look; needs protective coating |
| **Travertine** | Good – natural cemented stone | Moderate | Medium | Natural, warm tones; good for steps or low‑profile art |

### Bottom line
* **If longevity and low maintenance are top priorities** → choose **granite**.  
* **If you want intricate detail and don’t mind higher upkeep** → choose **marble** or **limestone**.  

Consider your local climate (acidic rain, temperature swings) and whether you’re willing to apply sealants or perform periodic cleaning.
